entries.title: Web browsers take center stage
entries.quote: 2005 will see much activity around the web browser. There will be more competition, more choice and more functionality.
entries.subject: Web browsers
entries.note: Secondary copy: Mondaq republication of the full Deloitte Technology report (2 February 2005).

entries.title: Fuel cells debut
entries.quote: 2005 will see the first commercial launch of ethanol-based fuel cells, both as standalone products and as the integrated power source for leading-edge consumer products.
entries.subject: Fuel cells for portable devices
entries.note: Secondary copy: Mondaq republication of the full Deloitte Technology report (2 February 2005).

entries.title: Super small technology. Huge returns
entries.quote: Nanotechnology – one of the most talked about but least understood technologies of the 21st century – will become increasingly mainstream in 2005.
entries.subject: Nanotechnology
entries.note: Secondary copy: Mondaq republication of the full Deloitte Technology report (2 February 2005).

entries.title: Connected devices under siege
entries.quote: Massive growth in the number of connected devices – from PCs and mobile phones to digital music players and gaming consoles – will cause a corresponding leap in electronic viruses and other malicious attacks.
entries.subject: Malware
entries.note: Secondary copy: Mondaq republication of the full Deloitte Technology report (2 February 2005).

entries.title: The robot invasion
entries.quote: After decades in science fiction, in 2005 robots will increasingly become an accepted part of our daily lives.
entries.subject: Household robots
entries.note: Secondary copy: Mondaq republication of the full Deloitte Technology report (2 February 2005).

entries.title: Mesh networks hit the streets
entries.quote: By the end of 2005, wireless mesh networks will have appeared in several major urban centers throughout Northern Europe, the United States and Asia.
entries.subject: Mesh networking
entries.note: Secondary copy: Mondaq republication of the full Deloitte Technology report (2 February 2005).

entries.title: Flat screen frenzy
entries.quote: In 2005, consumers will spend billions of dollars on liquid crystal displays (LCDs) and plasma flat panel screens, fueling strong market growth – particularly for large format devices such as televisions and computer monitors.
entries.metric: consumer spend on flat panel screens
entries.subject: Flat-panel displays
entries.note: Secondary copy: Mondaq republication of the full Deloitte Technology report (2 February 2005).

entries.title: Digital crime runs rampant
entries.quote: 2005 will see a rapid increase in electronic forms of identification, as governments around the world move to replace paper-based IDs with digital products. ... yet identify theft and other digital crimes will continue to wreak havoc.
entries.subject: Digital identity and cybercrime
entries.note: Secondary copy: Mondaq republication of the full Deloitte Technology report (2 February 2005). Second sentence from the report's summary.

entries.title: The space race moves into the private sector
entries.quote: First, there is likely to be an acceleration of the shift from the public to private sector, with public space agencies under increasing pressure to open up the market for launch vehicles and services.
entries.subject: Commercial spaceflight
entries.note: Secondary copy: Mondaq republication of the full Deloitte Technology report (2 February 2005).

entries.title: Quantum computing gets closer to reality
entries.quote: Quantum computers, which are expected to be many orders of magnitude faster than today's fastest supercomputers, will take a few important steps closer to commercial reality.
entries.subject: Quantum computing
entries.note: Secondary copy: Mondaq republication of the full Deloitte Technology report (2 February 2005). Quote from the report's summary.

notes: 4th edition by count from 2002. 'TMT Trends: Predictions, 2005 - A focus on the technology sector'; ten predictions stated in the foreword, all ten captured. Computerworld (20 January 2005) calls it 'the company's first publication of technological predictions', which fits Deloitte's statement that the series began in 2001 with ten predictions about mobile telephony. The 2005 Media and Telecommunications reports, if published, were not found. None of the ten headlines carries a number.
